questions.question: A PM sends a founder a well-researched document on a dependency that loses support in ten weeks. It gives two approaches with balanced pros and cons and ends with "happy to discuss Thursday." Why does nothing happen for three weeks?
options: The document contained no decision, so the cheapest available response was to schedule a meeting
The founder did not understand the technical risk well enough to act
The two options were too similar in cost to choose between
The document should have been shorter and more visual
questions.explanation: Balanced options with no recommendation ask the reader to supply both the position and the request. B is the tempting answer because it explains inaction by a gap in the reader, and it lets the author keep the document — but the memo never asked for anything, so there was nothing to say yes or no to.

questions.question: Two engineers disagree with your recommended approach. What handling of that dissent most increases your influence with the decision-maker?
options: Leave it out; internal disagreement is noise at the executive level and can be handled separately
Mention that "some concerns were raised about timing" and note that they were addressed
Name them, state their case in a form they would sign, say what would make them right, and say what you did about it
Present both positions with equal weight and let the executive choose between them
questions.explanation: The reader's real question is how much they have to check themselves; surfaced dissent answers it in your favour. B is the common compromise and it is worse than omission — the reader can tell an argument was softened. D abandons the recommendation, which returns you to the status-update failure.

questions.question: Which line does the most work at the end of an executive memo?
options: "Let me know if you have any questions or want to discuss further"
"I recommend we proceed and will keep you updated on progress"
"I'd welcome your thoughts before we finalize the approach"
"If I do not hear otherwise by Tuesday the 14th, we start on the split plan on Wednesday"
questions.explanation: D converts silence into a decision and makes the cost of delay visible. The most common failure of upward communication is not rejection but nothing happening, and A and C both leave that outcome available. B is the tempting one — it looks decisive, but with no date it gives the reader nothing to respond to before the option expires.

questions.question: A PM is about to escalate a decision that, under the team's own decision-rights map, is theirs to make. What does the model say?
options: Escalate anyway; keeping executives informed of significant calls is good practice
Escalate, since a second opinion on a consequential decision reduces risk
Apply the cover test — would this memo exist if they were confident? If not, decide and inform
Rewrite the memo as a note-only update so it does not read as an escalation
questions.explanation: A memo written from low confidence about a decision you own is a request for company, and readers learn to detect it. D is the tempting answer because it is technically honest and keeps the executive informed — but it still spends the reader's attention to relieve the author's discomfort, and the decision is still not made.

questions.question: An engineering lead carries the consequence of a recommendation but does not decide it. When should they see the memo?
options: Before the decision-maker, so their objection travels inside the memo rather than around it
At the same time as the decision-maker, so nobody is given an advantage
After the decision, so the recommendation is not weakened before it is heard
Only if they ask, since the decision is not theirs
questions.explanation: Sequence is what turns a peer's disagreement into content rather than an ambush. B is the tempting distractor — simultaneous circulation feels even-handed and transparent, but it gives the consequence-carrier no route to object except in front of the decision-maker, which is exactly when their objection is aimed at you rather than at the argument.
